edges.evidence: Sly Stone cited James Brown as a primary influence; There's a Riot Goin' On's drum machine-centered approach extends Brown's 'the beat is the song' doctrine into darker, more introspective territory.
George Clinton has repeatedly cited James Brown as the foundational influence for P-Funk's rhythmic vocabulary; Bootsy Collins played for James Brown before joining Parliament-Funkadelic.

Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards built Chic's rhythmic discipline on James Brown's foundational funk vocabulary; the locked bass-and-guitar interplay of Chic is a direct evolution of Brown's JBs rhythm section approach.

Sly Stone's 1971 drum-machine funk and stripped-down darkness are widely cited in funk historiography as a bridge between James Brown and the late-70s disco-soul that fed Studio 54; the nocturnal emotional register and four-on-the-floor pulse of Miss You trace through this lineage.

Parliament-Funkadelic were regular presences at Studio 54 and synonymous with the disco-funk milieu Jagger absorbed in 1977-78; both P-Funk's cosmic hedonism and the Stones' Some Girls sessions are documented within the same New York club-culture moment.

Chic's earlier work and Bernard Edwards' bass approach were already on the Studio 54 floor when Miss You was being shaped in 1977-78. The relationship is not literal sampling but shared Studio 54 idiom — Bill Wyman went 'to quite a few clubs' (per engineer Chris Kimsey) to internalize the same bass language Chic was building.

Saturday Night Fever (1977) and Some Girls (1978) are exact contemporaries; both represent major acts translating disco's four-on-the-floor pulse, though the Bee Gees dissolved into disco where the Stones kept rock's musculature audible.

Bowie's 1975 'plastic soul' pivot at Sigma Sound Studios preceded the Stones' disco move by three years and established the template: a white British rock star performing Black American rhythmic idioms without fully abandoning their rock identity.

John Deacon's bass line for 'Another One Bites the Dust' is documented as directly inspired by Chic's 'Good Times'; Miss You and the Queen track represent the same 1978-1980 phenomenon — a major rock band's bass player driving a disco-funk pivot — making this a well-documented parallel translation.

Both released in 1978; both represent rock acts deliberately crossing into disco territory while maintaining their rock-band identity. Heart of Glass and Miss You are the two best-known examples of the rock-disco crossover from that year.

Both released in 1978 by British rock artists based in the US pursuing disco crossover; Rod Stewart's 'Do Ya Think I'm Sexy?' reached US #1 in 1979, completing the same translation as Miss You but with less critical credit.

Talking Heads/Eno's Remain in Light (1980) absorbed the same rhythmic precision and studio layering approach as Chic, but filtered through Afrobeat and art-rock rather than disco — parallel translation of similar source material.

Devo formed explicitly as a reaction against what they saw as the devolution of rock into disco; Q: Are We Not Men? (1978) is a deliberate inversion of the Miss You cultural moment, choosing mechanical de-funk over natural groove.

Grace Jones occupied the same Studio 54 cultural space as Jagger; her work with Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare brought reggae/dub into the disco-rock crossover moment from the Jamaican perspective, while Miss You represented the rock-world's view of the same space.

Prince's rock-funk synthesis on Purple Rain extends the rock×funk translation to its logical conclusion; where Miss You kept the layers visible, Prince internalized them so completely they became indistinguishable — the descent one generation further.

edges.evidence: Flea has explicitly cited James Brown and Parliament-Funkadelic as the primary influences on his bass approach; Blood Sugar Sex Magik is the 90s rock-funk synthesis that descends directly from the Brown-to-disco-to-Miss You lineage.

Nile Rodgers (co-founder of Chic) was recruited to play guitar on 'Get Lucky' and other Random Access Memories tracks; Daft Punk explicitly credited Chic as the inspiration for the album's live-instrumentation approach. Personnel-level documented descent.

James Murphy has cited the late-70s rock-meets-disco moment — exemplified by Miss You — as a formative influence on LCD Soundsystem's aesthetic; 'All My Friends' shares the slow-burn disco pulse and hedonistic melancholy of Miss You, a lineage Murphy has discussed in multiple interviews.
